topStories.headline: Governor's Funding Threat Over Development Law Rattles Wasatch County
topStories.dek: After the county rejected a 144-lot development on state trust land, Gov. Spencer Cox's housing adviser threatened to withhold $2.1 million in annual road funding — a move that drew outrage from local leaders and residents.
topStories.body:
The latest chapter in Wasatch County's running battle with state officials over growth and housing law came to a head in late August and continued reverberating this week. After county leaders rejected a proposal by Philo Development to build 144 five-acre lots on Utah Trust Lands Administration property east of Heber City, Gov. Spencer Cox's senior housing adviser Steve Waldrip appeared at a Heber City Council meeting on Aug. 18 and delivered a stark message: the county's state road funding — roughly $2.1 million per year in B and C road allocations — was now at risk.

Waldrip's comments, invoking the governor's authority, touched off immediate anger. Heber City Council member Yvonne Barney told Waldrip at the meeting that threats do not go over well in the community and called for more open conversation. Utah News Dispatch reported receiving multiple emails from alarmed residents demanding answers about the governor's approach to local governance.

The dispute is also tangled up with SB258, a 2024 state law that allows up to three landowners in unincorporated areas to petition to form their own preliminary municipality, effectively bypassing county land-use authority. Philo Development has been pursuing such a designation — called Wasatch Highlands — for roughly 3,500 acres of privately held land adjacent to the trust-land parcel. The Wasatch County Council passed a resolution this month calling on the Legislature to repeal SB258, and County Manager Dustin Grabau has been rallying other counties — including Summit, Morgan, and Grand — to join that effort.

A subsequent meeting between county officials and the governor's office appears to have de-escalated the immediate threat. Grabau said the session was cordial and that he was able to 'correct' what he described as an 'untrue rumor' that the county intended to defy state law outright. No state funds have been withheld. Nonetheless, Grabau confirmed that Wasatch County would continue pushing for the law's repeal, and residents and council members alike have said the episode raised troubling questions about the use of state financial leverage to steer local land-use decisions.

topStories.headline: Bear Cub Near Heber Airport Captured, Then Euthanized After Biting Officer
topStories.dek: A young black bear spotted wandering alone near the Heber Valley Airport on Wednesday was safely caught at first, but was later put down after it bit a state wildlife officer during handling.
topStories.body:
What began as an unusual wildlife call on Wednesday morning ended in a grim outcome by Thursday. At approximately 9:40 a.m. on September 23, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources received a report of a young black bear near the Heber Valley Airport. Wasatch County Sheriff's Office deputies, an animal control officer, and a Department of Natural Resources Law Enforcement officer all responded. The cub was described by the Wasatch County Sheriff's Office as appearing 'lost and confused,' with no mother bear anywhere in the vicinity.

After deputies helped secure the cub with a catch pole and placed it in a live transport crate, the animal underwent evaluation. During the process, it bit a DNR officer. Under state policy, wildlife officials euthanized the bear and sent it to the Utah Public Health Laboratory to be tested for rabies, the Park Record reported on September 25.

The incident is part of a broader pattern across Utah this year. Bear sightings have more than doubled statewide compared to 2025, with state agencies reporting 168 bear incidents through late August alone versus 83 for all of 2025. The Utah Division of Wildlife Resources attributes the surge to drought conditions that have reduced natural food sources at higher elevations, pushing bears into lower-elevation communities. Wasatch County officials are reminding residents to keep a safe distance from wildlife, secure trash, and stay alert outdoors as bears continue to range through the valley this fall.

topStories.headline: Heber City Must Scrap Planned 4.2% Property Tax Increase After Missing State Notice Requirement
topStories.dek: The Utah State Tax Commission blocked the city's approved fiscal year 2027 property tax bump because the city failed to post required information on its website — a mistake that cannot be corrected mid-year.
topStories.body:
Heber City will have to operate without roughly $154,000 in additional revenue this fiscal year after the Utah State Tax Commission ruled that the city's 4.2 percent property tax increase for FY2027 cannot be imposed. The increase had been unanimously approved by city staff on August 18, but a review by the state commission found that Heber City failed to post a required combined city-and-county tax statement on its website for the mandated 14-day period before a public hearing — a new rule added during the 2026 legislative session.

City Manager Matt Brower told KPCW that the decision from the state cannot be appealed or protested, and that because the fiscal year is already underway, there is no remedy available. The city will instead roll back expenditures by 4.2 percent across each department. Brower said the city had sent notices to property owners and included the information in staff reports and council meeting materials, but the online posting requirement was missed.

The failed increase would have added about $15 to the annual tax bill on an $850,000 home. Brower has said the city's FY2027 budget was already conservative and that cutting it further will require negotiations over which expenditures can be deferred. The situation echoes a 2025 episode in which 39 cities, school districts, and special service districts statewide — including Henefer and Oakley in the Wasatch Back — had their tax increases denied under earlier rounds of new state rules.

moreNews.headline: State Audit Flags Recurring Election Compliance Issues in Wasatch County
moreNews.body: A report from the Utah Office of the Legislative Auditor General, published September 15, found repeated but relatively minor compliance shortcomings in how Wasatch County ran its 2026 primary election. Auditors found that the county completed only one of two recommended post-election audit steps, one of three chain-of-custody recommendations, and none of its reconciliation recommendations. Specific issues included untrained audit participants, inconsistent signature audits, a ballot processing room still lacking required camera coverage, and drop boxes without security seals. Auditors also identified one double vote — a voter who cast both a mail-in ballot and an in-person ballot — noting it was likely the only such instance statewide. Wasatch County Clerk-Auditor Joey Granger acknowledged the findings and said she will 'strive to ensure strong and effective election controls.' The newly elected clerk-auditor-elect separately pledged to address the issues ahead of the November general election.

moreNews.headline: Utah Supreme Court Weighs Final Outcome of Heber Valley Temple Dispute
moreNews.body: Heber Valley is waiting on the Utah Supreme Court's ruling after the court heard oral arguments on September 4 in the long-running lawsuit over the planned Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints temple east of downtown Heber. Attorneys for Wasatch County and the Church argued that county officials followed proper procedures by approving the 210-foot-tall, 88,000-square-foot temple through a legislative development agreement, while the petitioners — a group of Red Ledges homeowners — contend the approval violated local zoning rules that limit new buildings to 35 feet from natural grade in the residential zone. The Supreme Court allowed construction to continue while it weighs the appeal, meaning the church is proceeding at its own risk. A ruling in favor of the petitioners could require the structure to be torn down.
